resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should require technology companies to provide lawful access to encrypted communications.

contentions.text:
I'm arguing against the resolution, and my contention is about cybersecurity risk. Here's the fundamental problem: mandating lawful access to encrypted communications would create exploitable vulnerabilities that sophisticated adversaries can weaponize. 

Here's how this works. A backdoor, by definition, is "a method that bypasses normal authentication and encryption in a computer system, application, or network device, providing unauthorized remote access while remaining hidden from standard security measures." Once the government requires these backdoors to exist in encryption systems, they become targets. We've already seen this in practice. The threat actor UNC5221 maintained backdoor access to US legal firms and technology companies for an average of 393 days without detection. That's over a year of undetected infiltration. If we mandate government backdoors, we're essentially handing adversaries the same entry points law enforcement would use.

The impact is severe. Any backdoor we build for lawful access becomes a permanent vulnerability in our infrastructure. Foreign intelligence services, criminal organizations, and hostile actors would all exploit these same weaknesses. We'd be systematically undermining the encryption that protects American businesses, government communications, and critical infrastructure—all in the name of security.

contentions.text: I'm going to argue that mandated backdoors fundamentally destroy the security guarantees encryption provides to everyone. Here's why this matters: client-side scanning doesn't just create a technical loophole—it obliterates the entire premise of end-to-end encryption. According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, "client-side scanning fundamentally undermines end-to-end encryption, and obliterates our right to private spaces. If the government has access to one of the 'ends' of an end-to-end encrypted communication, that communication is no longer safe and secure." Once you give government access to one endpoint, the encryption is broken. It doesn't matter how carefully we write the law or how good the intentions are. The security architecture collapses. And here's the cascading impact: this sets a precedent that authoritarian regimes will exploit. The same source notes that "it sets a dangerous precedent to demand similar data from other companies, and provides a runway for other authoritarian governments to issue comparable orders." So we're not just weakening American security—we're handing a blueprint to autocrats worldwide to demand identical backdoors from the same companies. That means dissidents, journalists, and vulnerable populations globally lose their only protection against state surveillance. We cannot trade away fundamental encryption for the illusion of lawful access.

contentions.text:
I want to present a fundamental technical problem with this resolution. The mandate assumes that technology companies can actually comply with lawful access requirements, but the architecture of modern encryption makes that impossible for an entire class of products.

Here's the problem: zero-knowledge encryption systems are designed so that only users hold the encryption keys. The service provider literally cannot access the data, even if they wanted to. According to AxCrypt's documentation, "Only you have access to your encryption keys; even AxCrypt cannot access your data." This means there is no technical pathway for the provider to comply with a government access order. You cannot give someone access to something you do not possess.

The impact is that this mandate would be completely unenforceable against zero-knowledge systems. Companies using this architecture could simply say they are technically unable to comply, and they would be telling the truth. So we would end up with a law that applies only to some encryption products while others operate completely outside its reach. That makes the entire regulatory framework ineffective. We cannot require what is technically impossible, and we cannot regulate an industry when half the market uses architecture that makes compliance impossible.
